It signed the union of Florence in 1439, which monks, clergy and people at home rejected. It fell with the City on 29 May 1453 and went on, under a new patriarch, as the church of the Orthodox under Ottoman rule.
prose_changes.reason: The old summary carried build notes ('treated separately', 'a clean two-way handoff') and said the patriarchal church 'repudiates' Florence at home; before 1453 the church itself proclaimed the union (Leonard of Chios, December 1452), while monks, clergy and people rejected it.

Within months of the conquest the sultan installed Gennadios Scholarios as patriarch, and the church became the governing institution of the Orthodox population under Ottoman rule for the next four centuries — a continuous line reaching the Ecumenical Patriarchate of today. The union of Florence was formally repudiated and is still a live memory in Orthodox-Catholic relations. prose_changes.new: The church outlived the empire. Soon after the conquest the sultan had Gennadios Scholarios made patriarch. For four centuries the church led the Orthodox under Ottoman rule. Its line runs on to the patriarch in Istanbul today. The Greeks never truly took up the union of Florence. It is still a sore memory between Orthodox and Catholics. Some scholars left for Italy, Bessarion among them. They took Greek books and Greek learning with them into the Renaissance.
prose_changes.reason: A formal repudiation has no vendored or repo-cited source. Leonard of Chios, writing to the pope in 1453, says the Greeks kept the union in word and denied it in deed.

prose_changes.old: Sergius of Radonezh withdrew into the woods north of Moscow in the 1340s to live alone. Within a generation the monastery that grew up around him had sent out disciples who founded dozens more, pushing ever deeper into the northern forests in what later Russians called the northern Thebaid. The texts followed — Epiphanius the Wise's life of Sergius, the skete rules of Nil Sorsky. And so did the art, since Andrei Rublev's Trinity was painted in Sergius's memory for his own monastery. The period also produced the sharpest argument in Russian church history. Nil Sorsky and the non-possessors held that monasteries should own no land and no peasants and should live by their own labor, while Joseph of Volotsk and the possessors held that endowed monasteries could feed the poor, train clergy and carry the church's work. The possessors won it at the council of 1503. In the middle of all this, in 1448, Russian bishops elected their own metropolitan without waiting on Constantinople — the beginning of an independent Russian church.
prose_changes.new: Sergius of Radonezh withdrew into the woods north of Moscow in the 1340s to live alone. A monastery grew up around him. Within a generation his disciples had founded dozens more, pushing ever deeper into the northern forests. Later Russians called this the northern Thebaid. The texts followed: Epiphanius the Wise's life of Sergius, and the skete rules of Nil Sorsky. So did the art. Andrei Rublev painted his Trinity in Sergius's memory, for Sergius's own monastery. The same years saw the sharpest quarrel in Russian church history. Nil Sorsky and the non-possessors held that monasteries should own no land and no peasants. Monks should live by their own work. Joseph of Volotsk and the possessors held that rich monasteries could feed the poor, train clergy and carry the church's work. The monasteries kept their lands. Soon after 1496 Grand Prince Ivan planned to take them, but the metropolitan talked him out of it. In the middle of all this, in 1448, Russian bishops chose their own metropolitan without waiting on Constantinople. It was the beginning of an independent Russian church.
prose_changes.reason: No vendored or repo-cited source carries a council of 1503 deciding the quarrel. Mouravieff's history shows the outcome: soon after Simon became metropolitan (1496), the grand prince meant to take church lands and the metropolitan dissuaded him.

prose_changes.old: Sergius of Radonezh withdrew into the forests north of Moscow in the 1340s to live alone, and within a generation his monastery's disciples had founded dozens more, pushing deep into what Russians called the northern Thebaid. The era's sharpest argument was over monastic wealth: Nil Sorsky and the non-possessors wanted monks poor and silent, Joseph of Volotsk and the possessors wanted monasteries endowed and socially useful, and the possessors won at a council in 1503. Andrei Rublev painted his Trinity icon, now the most famous icon ever made, for Sergius's own monastery.
prose_changes.new: Sergius of Radonezh withdrew into the forests north of Moscow in the 1340s to live alone. Within a generation his disciples had founded dozens more houses, deep in what Russians called the northern Thebaid. The era's sharpest quarrel was over what monks should own. Nil Sorsky and the non-possessors wanted monks poor and silent. Joseph of Volotsk and the possessors wanted monasteries rich enough to serve the people. In the end the monasteries kept their lands. Andrei Rublev painted his Trinity for Sergius's own monastery. It is now the most famous icon ever made.
prose_changes.reason: As in the long description: the council of 1503 has no vendored or repo-cited source; the monasteries keeping their lands has.

prose_changes.old: Nothing continued. After the Ottoman conquest the krstjani disappear from the record within a generation or two, absorbed into Islam, Catholicism and Orthodoxy, and no later church claims descent from them. What remains is inscriptional and archaeological: charters and grave inscriptions naming djeds and gosts, and the stećci, the great carved limestone tombstones of medieval Bosnia and its neighbors. Though those were raised by Catholics and Orthodox as well, and the once-popular idea that they are specifically a Bosnian Church monument is no longer accepted. The church's other legacy is the argument about it, which became part of Bosnian national self-understanding in the twentieth century and is still running.
prose_changes.new: Nothing continued. After the Ottoman conquest the krstjani vanish from the written sources within a generation or two. Many seem to have become Muslims; no surviving text shows where the rest went. No later church claims descent from them. What remains is on parchment and stone. Charters and grave inscriptions name djeds and gosts. And there are the stećci, the great carved limestone tombstones of medieval Bosnia and its neighbors. Catholics and Orthodox raised those too, and the once-popular idea that they are a Bosnian Church monument is no longer accepted. The church's other legacy is the argument about it, which is still running.
prose_changes.reason: Absorption 'into Islam, Catholicism and Orthodoxy': Evans (1877, lines 2456-2462) supports the turn to Islam, citing Montalbano; no vendored or repo-cited source shows the others, so that part is qualified. 'Part of Bosnian national self-understanding in the twentieth century' has no vendored or repo-cited source and is removed. The sentence fragment ('. Though those were raised') is mended.
